The potential difference (p.d.) across the resistor is 3.3 V.
What is the resistance of the lamp?

hints: Notice the two components are in series, so first find the current through the resistor when its $V = 3.3$ $\text{V}$ from the straight-line resistor $I$-$V$ graph.
That same current must flow through the lamp, so look across to the curved filament lamp $I$-$V$ graph and read the lamp voltage that gives this current.
Remember the lamp is non-ohmic, so calculate its resistance at that point only with $R = V/I$ using the lamp voltage and the common current.
walkthrough: In series the current $I$ is the same in the resistor and the lamp, so find $I$ from the resistor data.
On the resistor $I$-$V$ graph, $V = 3.3$ $\text{V}$ corresponds to $I \approx 0.30$ $\text{A}$. The graph is linear through the origin, about $0.09$ $\text{A}$ per volt.
Use this same $I \approx 0.30$ $\text{A}$ on the filament lamp $I$-$V$ graph. Read horizontally from $0.30$ $\text{A}$ to the curve, then down to the voltage axis.
Resistance of the lamp at this operating point is $R = V_{lamp}/I = 4.0/0.30 \approx 13.3$ $\Omega$.
Rounded to the given options this is about $14$ $\Omega$. This is option D

A.explanation: This is about $1/14$ $\Omega^{-1}$, the reciprocal of the lamp resistance, not $R = V/I$ in $\Omega$.

B.explanation: This is far too small and does not match $V/I$ for the lamp at the common series current of about $0.30$ $\text{A}$.

C.explanation: This uses the resistor p.d. of $3.3$ $\text{V}$ divided by $0.30$ $\text{A}$, but $3.3$ $\text{V}$ is across the resistor, not the lamp.

D.explanation: At the series current of about $0.30$ $\text{A}$ the lamp p.d. is about $4.0$ $\text{V}$, so $R = 4.0/0.30 \approx 14$ $\Omega$.
